meaningMnemonic: This radical is a cage because it's covered on all sides but one (the one open side is where the cage door or gate is). There's nothing inside this cage because there's no gate, and whatever was inside has gotten out. I hope it wasn't rabid...

This is a cape , like the kind a superhero would wear. Use your imagination to picture a hero facing left, with a cape tied around their neck and hanging down their back. With that cape on, they're ready to save the world!

This looks like the kind of building you'd find in a Japanese capital . See the ornate roof and the stone foundation flaring out underneath, like a castle? The emperor lives in there. And wherever the emperor lives automatically becomes the capital city. That's why this radical is capital. Alternatively, you can use the radical parts and imagine a giant lid on the pot that will feed the mouths of all the small people in the capital.

This is the radical for cloud . See how the cloud is puffy on the bottom but has two lines up top? That's because a plane flew through it. It was a nice cloud to hang out privately in, until that darn plane came through and ruined it. So much for your private cloud!

This radical is made up of two slightly different versions of the spoon radical. Look closely at these two spoons. Compare their differences, like the different angles in the bends of the spoons. It's like one of those "spot the difference" games where you compare two similar pictures. But this time it's with spoons.
Flying to the sun with wings is easy ! Or so Icarus thinks. Someone should probably tell him…
This looks like a hook , like the kind a pirate would wear. The flat line shows where the hand was cut off, and the hook is right above, ready to take its place. Yarrrr.

This radical looks like a horse . See the long, thick neck with the mane flowing to the right? What might look like a wing is actually the horse's four legs and its tail hanging down. Don't confuse this radical with the bird radical ( 鳥 ). They look similar, but this one doesn't have the little feather sticking out of the top of its head!
This is a net , spread out over the water. Imagine all the fish you can catch in this net!

Most of this radical is just the rice radical, but the top part is something coming to cut the rice from its stalk. That, my friend, is the sickle . See how the rice is still there? That's because it's in motion. The sickle is literally doing the cutting RIGHT NOW! (And don't confuse this with the grain 禾 radical!)

This is the snake radical. See the head at the top with its long skinny body stretching down from it? Don't confuse this with 己 (oneself) — the snake has an extra line behind its head to connect to the rest of its body.

You find a coffin on the sun. It's burnt to a crisp from the heat, but there's definitely someone in there. You wonder who this mysterious someone might have been. Whoever they were, they got a fancy sun burial, so they really must've been someone (or shall we say, sun-one ?).

This is the radical for suit , like when something suits you. You find a hat on the ground, and when you pick it up, there's a mouth underneath. "It suits you! It suits you!" the mouth says. You try the hat on, and yup — it really suits! It's weird getting fashion advice from a random mouth, but hey, it wasn't wrong.

Stick a table on top of a stool and you end up with a very dangerous weapon . Imagine hitting someone with this thing! Or, even better, imagine making someone sit on it. They'd be crushed mentally and emotionally and whatnot. Now that's a scary weapon.

"Does the bamboo shirt suit me?" you ask... but nobody will answer . Hints Shout "PLEASE ANSWER ME!" a few times to get the idea of "answer" in your head. What you really want is an answer, whether it's bad or good, but nobody's willing to say anything because you look so terrible.
readingMnemonic: You pull out a quarter ( こた ) and offer it to whoever will give you an answer . Hints With this shiny quarter in your hand, everyone is giving you their answer. Yay for bribery!

meaningMnemonic: Under a cliff there's a stool . If someone has a stool deep inside a cliff, they are most likely pretty anti -society, hiding away like that. Hints Imagine someone who looks super anti-social (and a little feral). Ask them why they're sitting on this stool inside a cliff. They reply it's because they hate people. They're anti-people. In fact, they're anti-everything.
readingMnemonic: Turns out, when you go to this guy and pull off his beard, its the anti -hero from Star Wars, Han ( はん ) Solo! What is Han doing here, so hidden away? He's obviously hiding from Jabba because he doesn't want to get frozen in carbonite again. Hints Make sure you get to the point where you pull this anti-social guy's beard off, to reveal Han Solo beneath. Be surprised... not just because he's Han Solo, but because he's real, too! Maybe you can yell out "Han! Your people need you!"

meaningMnemonic: When your self goes down a slide and hits a barb , it's a painful reminder that you have a body . Sometimes people think their self is just some kind of floating, disembodied consciousness, but getting a barb stuck in oneself while going down a slide will quickly remind one of one's bodily existence. Hints Imagine hurtling down a slide, your inner self reveling in the joy of the moment. Then, you hit a sharp barb — OUCH!!! Suddenly, you're very conscious of your body again.
readingMnemonic: What part of your body did the barb get stuck in? Your shin ( しん ). That pointy little barb dug deep into your shin and made you painfully aware of the fact that oneself and one's body are inextricable. Hints Feel the sharp pain in your shin as it radiates through your body. It kinda sucks, but in a way it's reassuring proof of the physical existence of oneself.

meaningMnemonic: Wolverine is going down a slide and from your mouth you scream, "Hey, buddy ! Watch it with that slide, it's really fast and you might hurt yourself, buddy!" You're a really good buddy to Wolverine. He also happens to be the local ruler of these lands. You make it a habit to befriend the local strongmen, just in case… No wonder you're so buddy-buddy with all the rulers around here. Hints Imagine having all the local rulers as your buddies, all the influence you would have. You might end up with everyone wanting to be your buddy.
readingMnemonic: The biggest perk of having Wolverine as your buddy is that he teaches you kun g fu ( くん ). Wolverine wants you, his good buddy, to know how to defend yourself. That's why he uses his martial arts knowledge to train you in kung fu every day after he gets done playing on the slide. Hints There's no better way to bond with a good buddy than some daily kung fu sparring.

meaningMnemonic: Your nation's flag sits on top of a cape d mouth . This is the symbol for the " Bureau of Secret Things." It's a special department of your government made to keep things hidden. Hints The cape covering the mouth represents how this bureau never talks about their secrets. The flag represents your country. Think about all the cool secret things the Bureau of Secret Things must have.
readingMnemonic: The bureau 's best-kept secret is cloaking devices that cloak you ( きょく ) with the press of a button. Hints Now, this mnemonic isn’t perfectly close, but the goal is to get you close enough in your brain so that you can remember きょく later. If you can get to CLOAK YOU, then you can get to きょく much easier than just trying to get there from scratch. So imagine working in this bureau and getting to cloak yourself all the time.

meaningMnemonic: Here's a net full of of shellfish that you can buy . You can't just buy loose shellfish. You can only buy the ones that are in the net, bagged up and ready for your money. Hints Imagine looking over a bunch of different kinds of shellfish wrapped in nets. Think about which ones you want to buy.
readingMnemonic: You decide to buy as many shellfish as you can fit in your ca r ( か ). You keep buying until your car is completely full of shellfish before you stop. Cars are totally a realistic unit of measure. Hints Imagine buying an entire car's worth of shellfish. Mmm, delicious.

meaningMnemonic: Just like the radical, the kanji means capital . Hints Know your radicals!
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading きょう we use the old capital of Japan, Kyoto, which is spelled きょう と . It was the capital of Japan before Tokyo! Hints When you think of the capital, any capital, think of きょうと .

meaningMnemonic: A rain cloud is still a cloud ! It's probably going to rain on you soon though, so I hope you have a jacket or an umbrella. Hints Picture all of the different types of clouds in the sky. There are puffy white ones, heavy dark ones, and wispy thin ones. But they're all clouds.
readingMnemonic: You lie down and try to figure out what the cloud s are shaped like. The first cloud is shaped... like a coo l mo m ( くも ). She's wearing high pants, and holding a kid on each hip, but she's also listening to the latest music and using slang. Huh. You look to the next cloud and see... wait, another cool mom? Hints You look at each cloud and each one is a different cool mom. They're each doing different cool mom things. You suddenly don't want to look at the clouds anymore.

meaningMnemonic: The white ice tree is a magical tree that radiates an aura of comfort , ease , and pleasure , with its icy foliage tinkling like beautiful music whenever it sways in the breeze. Hints Close your eyes and feel the aura of comfort wash over you. Listen to the musical tinkling of the tree's icy branches, setting you at ease. You never want this pleasurable moment to end!
readingMnemonic: You want more of this aura of comfort , so you chop down the magic tree and build a clothing rack ( らく ) out of it. Then, you put the rack in your house so you can enjoy that fuzzy feeling of comfort and ease every time you go to hang something up. Hints Place a hanger on the rack. Feel the wave of pleasure that runs through you, and then bask in the afterglow of comfort and ease that it leaves behind. Now, go find something else to hang up on your rack. You need another hit of comfort and pleasure.

meaningMnemonic: Give rice to a woman in winter so she can count it. The woman will count each individual grain of rice, then tell you the amount or number of grains. Hints She has to count each grain in order to divvy up the rice supply and make it last the winter. Imagine the amount you get today — just a small number of grains. It's not a good time for you guys…
readingMnemonic: The rice this woman has to count is for your sou p ( すう ). It's important to ration! You may not be getting many grains — few enough to count on two hands, probably — but at least you can enjoy them in a nice, hot bowl of soup. Hints To remember that this is すう and not す , imagine the woman saying "soup" in a really drawn-out way, like "sooooouuuup." Try counting how many seconds it takes her to say it.

meaningMnemonic: You have at your disposal a tsunami to assassinate this person , or a hook . Which method will you choose? Decide now! Hints Have trouble with the decision. Which one? Tsunami will be big and cool, but a hook will be more discreet. How can you decide? Can you think of a neat way to decide this? You're like Two-Face deciding on how to kill Batman.
readingMnemonic: To remember the けつ reading, we always use the word "ketsup." It's a special mix of ketchup and catsup (yum): You finally decide . You're going to go with the tsunami... but not just any tsunami. You'll kill him with a tsunami of ketsu p ( けつ ). Hints Get everything ready to take your target down. How will you collect enough ketsup to make a ketsup tsunami? Where will you unleash it? You gotta decide on the ketsup logistics now.

meaningMnemonic: The leader of the master s gets to choose the place they dwell . So they reside in a huge mansion on the top of the mountain, surrounded by all the other masters in their smaller dwellings. Hints Picture the leader master who dwells in a big, beautiful dwelling. Everyone else is jealous.
readingMnemonic: She needs this big place to dwell so she has somewhere to store all of her jew els ( じゅう ). Masters always have lots of fancy, expensive things, and she has jewels. Hints Imagine opening the door to the leader master's dwelling and thousands of jewels come pouring out, whisking you off, down the mountain.

meaningMnemonic: You're in the rain , in a rice paddy , holding an umbrella . You're here because there's nothing else that's very tall around you. You want to get hit by electricity (aka lightning), to prove that it exists. Hints Imagine being hit by the electricity. Feel the powerful electric shock pulse through your body. You're like a crazier Ben Franklin out here.
readingMnemonic: After the electricity hits you, you feel your face. In it is a huge den t ( でん ). Hints Feel the indent in your face. It doesn't hurt, strangely, but it is pretty huge. Panic about this dent a bit.

meaningMnemonic: This kanji is just the tree radical three times. Just based off this, you should be able to figure it out. This kanji means " forest ." Hints Makes sense, because a bunch of individual trees is what makes up a forest!
readingMnemonic: One tree? No. Two trees? Not enough. I want more ( もり ) trees, please! Hints Keep repeating this pattern over and over, continually focusing in on how you need "more" trees to make this forest. For some reason the person working with you only goes up by one at a time, though, so you have to say it a lot (it'll help you to remember, anyways!).

meaningMnemonic: With top hat power , you're able to help anyone. Hints Imagine putting on your top hat and getting power from it. Then, you use that power to help someone. It's important to make the association that it's the top hat giving you the power to help that person. You're basically Frosty the Snow Man.
readingMnemonic: The person you help with your top hat power? It's Jo -Anne ( じょ ). Hints You can imagine saving her however you like. Perhaps she was under a car, and you used your top hat powers to help her out of that situation by lifting it above your head. Note: Jo-Anne is the character we're using with じょ reading mnemonics. She is short compared to Joe ( じょう ), the giant farmhand, which is how you'll differentiate the two similar readings.

meaningMnemonic: The horse radical and the horse kanji are exactly the same! Huzzah!
readingMnemonic: You are looking at a horse. It's looking at you. You try making horse noises at it, to get a reaction. Instead of reacting with a normal horse noise, it just makes sheep noises: " Baaa ," ( ば ) it says. "Baaaaa." Hints Feel the shock of this. It sounds just like a sheep, it's strange.

meaningMnemonic: There's a gate that the sun goes through at a regular interval . There is an interval of time in the sense that the sun goes through it at the same time every day. And there is an interval of space in the sense that it has to go through the space between the gate posts. Hints "Interval" is a weird word to remember, but just think of the sun going around the earth and through the gate like clockwork. Every 24 hours it passes through the gate, and each interval is exactly the same.
readingMnemonic: This method of keeping track of interval s of time was invented by the great Khans of Mongolia, specifically the most famous Khan of all: Genghis Khan ( かん ). Genghis Khan has had a huge impact on the world as we know it, especially the Eurasian continent of the past, so he's going to come up a lot from now on. Be prepared to get very familiar with him and his friends! Hints Picture Genghis Khan ordering his most skilled inventors and builders to create this special sun gate so they can harness the power of intervals, and all people under his rule can benefit from the accurate telling of time.

meaningMnemonic: Dirt makes it easy to identify your location . Even if you add an extra line to mark the ground, it's still easy. Keep that in mind and you can go from place to place. Hints Imagine looking at the dirt. It's a distinct color and texture, and you're able to identify your location just from that alone. Now draw that line on the ground and you'll always remember this place.
readingMnemonic: Knowing your location from dirt is quite a feat! Who taught you that? It was Joe ( じょう ), the big local farmhand. Despite being a bit weird, he can identify any place just from its dirt! Hints Remember Joe? He's our local farmhand who only has nine toes (from the 上 mnemonic). Imagine that guy explaining to you how to know your location from dirt. He may be a bit clumsy, but the man really knows his dirt.

meaningMnemonic: You're in a cage and you've been shot by an arrow . Obviously things are looking pretty bad. You need some medicine if you hope to live. Hints More specifically, antibiotics. Your wound is festering pretty badly.
readingMnemonic: When we need to remember the sound い we use the word "Eagle." You need your medicine really bad. Then, you look up. There's an ea gle ( い ) flying overhead. He has a package. It's medicine! You're saved! Hints Or, so you think. He just keeps circling and circling. Feel some hate for the eagle. Why isn't he dropping the medicine? You don't have long to live!

meaningMnemonic: There's a cross sticking out the top of the sun and another cross sticking out the bottom. The moon is off to the right. That's because it's the morning , which is when the sun and moon switch over. Those crosses are making sure the sun stays high in the sky for the rest of the day. Hints Imagine a sun attached up in the sky with two crosses, which act as scaffolding, and the moon gradually fading off to the right as the morning wears on.
readingMnemonic: Every morning you have Asa hi ( あさ ) beer for breakfast. Hints You watch the sun scaffolded by crosses, and the moon next to it, as you sip on your early-morning Asahi.

meaningMnemonic: Ice is what you're lack ing, so the next thing you need to do is go to the store and see if they have any. Nope, no ice. So, now you go to the next store. Is there ice here? Nope. Next! Hints Feel a little frustrated you can't find ice. Have the words " next next next" echoing through your head as you go from store to store, irritated.
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading じ , we used the word "Jesus" - Finally, when you're at the last store in existence, you decide it's time to pray to Je sus ( じ ), asking for a miracle. He comes down from the heavens with ice in his hands. Hints Imagine him coming down. Imagine your surprise. He hands you the ice, and it's cold. You thank him, and he flies away.

meaningMnemonic: You have to sickle the rice paddy today because it's your turn . This kanji also means number in a series , which is a lot like a turn. For example, you're number 3, so your turn will be number 3. Hints Go through in your mind the system your farm / village uses for deciding who has to sickle on any given day. It rotates, and it's a turn-based system. So, do you all stand in a line? Is there a calendar? Come up with something interesting, focusing on your turn in the process you come up with. It will be helpful to remember both the "number in a series" and "turn" meanings for the vocab coming up in the future.
readingMnemonic: This turn -based rice sickle system is a contest as well! But, you are disappointed to find out that you have been ban ned ( ばん ) from the game because of the performance enhancing steroids you've been taking. Hints Try to feel disappointed by this. Strange thing to feel disappointed by, but you were a great sickler. You were going to win the great prize, too (come up with something huge!), but now you're banned for the season.

meaningMnemonic: When a bunch of thread s are meet ing on paper (after you've dipped them in paint, say) they can create a masterpiece of a picture (or painting ). Hints It's unbelievable the kind of picture you're able to paint with just the tips of threads. So much detail. So artistic. If it helps, imagine that you drew the Mona Lisa, better than the original, only using this thread tool.
readingMnemonic: You tell someone you painted this masterpiece of a picture . Their response? " EH ( え )?!" Hints Tell a few more people about your picture. Have them all do the same surprised "Eh?!" reaction at your art skills.

meaningMnemonic: You're tearing this door down with an axe . You're absolutely crazy. "I HATE THIS PLACE !!" you keep yelling as you smash in the door. Hints Why do you hate this place, in particular? Come up with a great reason why to help you to remember this very broad kanji meaning.
readingMnemonic: You smash through the door and finally get inside the place , only to find some kind of sho w ( しょ ) going on. It's a circus show — elephants, tightrope walkers, bears on unicycles! The greatest show on earth, but why is it at this place? Hints Come up with a weird reason as to why the circus is at this place you hate so much. Why did you come here with your axe? Does it have something to do with the circus show?

meaningMnemonic: The poor alligator was taken far inland by a tsunami . Now his only source of water is a tiny pond that barely fits his body, and doesn't even provide much food. Hints Imagine the alligator riding the tsunami in. When he hits the ground, and the water recedes, he's all alone in a pond, but it doesn't provide much for him. Imagine him looking for food in the little, shallow pond. Imagine him trying to stay wet... it's just not a great situation to be in, unfortunately.
readingMnemonic: The worst part about this pond is that the only thing for the alligator to eat is chee se ( ち ). Cheese may be yummy for humans, but alligators hate it. They'd rather eat the cow the cheese came from. Sadly, this pond is full of cheese. Hints Picture an alligator crying in a pond full of cheese. It's eating a piece really slowly and weeping.

meaningMnemonic: You dig a hole nine times for your research . You should always do research with nine variables so you can compare them, and so there's an uneven number. Hints Imagine carefully digging a hole nine times, in nine different spots, so you can do your research. Hmm, I wonder what kind of research these holes are for…
readingMnemonic: Your research is on cu cumbers ( きゅう )! Hints Put nine full-grown cucumbers into their holes so you can research what happens next.

meaningMnemonic: Aim the scooter 's neck at the road ! Scooters are only meant for driving on street s and path s, and if you go the wrong way , you'll probably break your own neck! Hints Imagine riding your scooter down the road. You're carefully aiming the scooter's neck the right way so you don't end up going out of control and dying.
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading どう we use the word "doughnut." You're traveling down this road so fast that you don't see the giant dou ghnut ( どう ) that's rolling toward you until the last minute. You crash into it, and both you and the doughnut go tumbling down. Ahg, your neck! Hints Alternate ending: You do a sweet jump, go right through the doughnut hole, take a bite, and land safely back onto the road!

meaningMnemonic: You loiter around with a weapon because you're currently doing your service and duty to your country. You're standing guard outside, waiting just in case something will happen. Hints Imagine standing around with a weapon in your hands. It feels more like you're doing nothing, loitering around the wall, but this is how you offer your service to your country, so you have to do it.
readingMnemonic: You're about halfway through your service , when a yak ( やく ) walks by. It stops directly in front of you and grunts. "Excuse me, Mr. Yak, but it's my duty to escort you away from my country." Hints Somehow your duty has become pushing this stubborn, hairy yak away from the entrance to your country. You poke it in the butt with your weapon, but it doesn't seem to care.

meaningMnemonic: A stone lantern is an excellent way to sharpen anything, even in the dark. Your knives, your forks, your spoons, and even your sword. Hints Imagine walking around at night and you need to sharpen your sword. You walk up to a stone lantern and rub your sword all over it to sharpen it. Touch the blade. Indeed, it's been sharpened!
readingMnemonic: Why did you sharpen your blade? Because you are about to do battle with Ken ( けん ), the famous samurai warrior. Hints You'll want to remember this character, because he will come up many times throughout your WaniKani journey. Ken the samurai used to work for WaniKani, but then he went rogue because he thought WaniKani wasn't being radical enough. So now he wanders the website carrying his squid friend (who you'll meet later) in a bucket. To help you visualize him, imagine a samurai with armor made from crab shells, a helmet that is just an alligator head, and swords with crab claw hand guards. His great beard and mustache are styled in the shape of whatever kanji is giving you the most trouble at the time.

meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji are exactly the same, so this means someone . Hints Well, well… someone's lucky to not have to learn a new kanji.
readingMnemonic: If you don't know who someone is, odds are they're a sha man ( しゃ ). Only a shaman would have the mystical powers to obscure their own identity and pass themselves off as a mysterious, unknown "someone." Hints Think back on someone you met recently whose name or face you can't really remember. Hate to break it to you, but… they were a shaman.

meaningMnemonic: The branch radical and the branch kanji are the same! This kanji also means support . To remember it, think about a tree with lots of branches. The branches support each other and the trunk of the tree. If you were to climb the tree, the branches would be able to support your weight too! Hints Picture a branch supporting the weight of you, your entire family, and maybe a few friends.
readingMnemonic: You're happily sitting on this branch , letting it support all this weight, when a shee p ( し ) starts to climb the tree. A very, very big sheep. Uh oh... no no, sheep. If you get on this branch it won't be able to support all this weight!!! Hints The big sheep walks up the side of the tree with its weird hooves and starts to put its weight on the branch. "No no no!" you and your whole family scream. The branch can't support the weight of the sheep. It snaps! You all tumble to the ground. The end.

meaningMnemonic: Say it with your tongue . If you do, you'll be able to talk . You'll be able to speak . Hints Your problem is you weren't saying it with your tongue before. Once you start using your tongue, you're able to speak suddenly!
readingMnemonic: If something uses their tongue, it will be able to talk and speak . To prove this, you teach a wa lrus ( わ ) to use its tongue, and lo and behold, it speaks to you! Hints You decided to teach a walrus how to speak because it seemed like the hardest thing to teach, with its tusks and all that. It turned out to be really easy. Although, you may have picked the Justin Long walrus, by accident. Either way, this walrus can speak! And you definitely (probably) helped.

meaningMnemonic: In your fingers is a weapon , so you throw it. Maybe you're angry and you threw the weapon at a person you don't like. Maybe you're a pacifist and you threw it away so no one else could use it. Either way, when you have a weapon in your fingers you have to throw it. Hints Imagine a weapon in between your fingers. It doesn't matter what kind. Now feel the weight as you throw it.
readingMnemonic: You throw your weapon away because you're about to enter とう きょう and there are no weapons allowed there. There is, however, a big pile of thrown away weapons by the border, which is where you're throwing yours right now. Hints Imagine throwing the weapon in your fingers just before you walk into とうきょう . You can see the lights, smell the smells! Throw your weapons and your cares away!

meaningMnemonic: Writing and measurement stand versus one another. Writing is all about feeling and expression. Measurement is about cold hard numbers. Yep, in this world writing people are basically the opposite of measurement people. Which side are you on? Hints What's that, you say? It doesn't always have to be writing types versus measurement types? We can work together to create a better society? Nah, sorry, I'd rather it be me versus the world.
readingMnemonic: Whenever it's you versus someone else, you wear a tie ( たい ). Naturally, your tie is always the opposite color of your opponent's tie. Kinda like how political rivals wear different color ties when they debate. It's pretty silly, but at least your tie makes it clear that it's you versus them. Hints Think of someone you know who's your total opposite. Now imagine you're both in ties, but opposite colors, and you're debating… or fighting in a cage match or something.

meaningMnemonic: Remember 地下 , which is "below ground." Well, this is ground and above combined together, so I bet you can guess that this means above ground . But usually things above ground don't float (unless you're in space), so it's really on the ground .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: ここは、地上のフロアです。
sentences.english: This is a floor above ground.

sentences.japanese: ロケットは今、地上三千メートルにいる。
sentences.english: The rocket is now 3,000 meters above the ground.

sentences.japanese: 東京タワーは、地上から見上げると、大きさがよく分かりますね。
sentences.english: You can see the size of the Tokyo Tower if you look up from the ground.

meaningMnemonic: If you dwell in a place , that place is your address .
readingMnemonic: This word is made up of the on'yomi readings that you've already learned with the kanji. Have at it!

sentences.japanese: 次に、住所を入力して下さい。
手紙を出したいんですが、家の住所を教えてもらえませんか？
sentences.english: I'd like to mail out a letter, but can you tell me the address of the house?

sentences.japanese: 会社の住所は三丁目です。
sentences.english: The address of the company is 3-chome.

meaningMnemonic: When you help with what you say , you're giving advice . This word is commonly found in formal or professional contexts. In more casual settings, you can just use アドバイス (advise) instead.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: これは、お父さんからの助言です。
sentences.english: This is advice from my dad.

sentences.japanese: 社長は全てのスタッフに役に立つ助言をしました。
sentences.english: The president gave useful advice to all the staff.

sentences.japanese: 母は私に自立するための助言をしてくれました。
sentences.english: My mother advised me about being independent.

sentences.japanese: そのチョコレートをくれたら、助言をあげるわ。
sentences.english: I will give you advice, if you give me that chocolate.

meaningMnemonic: 米 means "rice," but remember how it can mean "America" too? Well, all America is exactly what it sounds like: all America . Just keep in mind that we're not talking about America as a continent here. This word specifically means the entire USA — no more, no less.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: When you stick this onto the end of another word that talks about an interval of time in some way, you're indicating the amount of time that has gone past. For example, 二年間 is "two years." 一時間 is "one hour." Any amount of time + 〜間 will make it an "amount of time" instead of just a specific time. Note that 〜間 can be omitted, especially in conversations, when it's clear that you're talking about a duration of time from the context. However, the exception is 時 . You always say 〜時間 to refer to the amount of hours, to differentiate from 〜時 ( 〜 o'clock).
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. This should save you at least 二分間 .

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the vocab word are the same, so this means body or oneself . It also refers to animal flesh sometimes, meaning the non-bone edible parts of animals, including seafood. It's the "mi" in sashimi! Wondering about the difference between 体 and 身 ? Basically, 体 is for the physical human (or animal) body as a whole, and is often used in relation to its condition or appearance. 身 can refer to a physical human body too, but unlike 体 , it's also used to refer to the self as an individual and, by extension, to one's social standing or circumstances.

You want to be the best yo-yoer there's ever been, so you're up with the dawn every morning, practicing your yo-yo skills while the competition sleeps. meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Don't confuse this with 〜間 which is similar in meaning but different in reading. The 〜間 means it's attached to something. This is a standalone word.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. 間 has two common kun'yomi readings, あいだ and ま . You haven't learned these readings yet, so here's an explanation of each reading and mnemonics to help you remember them: 間 is usually read as あいだ for a longer interval of time or general space between things. It's read as ま for a short burst of time or when defining a specific area, like a 茶の間 (the older name for a Japanese living room). You can remember this because time feels longer in Ida ho ( あいだ ). Any interval of time you spend there feels so long, because Idaho life moves so slowly. As soon as you cross the border and enter a new state, you call your ma ( ま ) to tell her you're finally out of that slooooow state, and the intervals of time feel shorter.

to go in between, to intervene

meaningMnemonic: You know the word 長い from a couple levels ago. This is like the word 大きい versus 大きさ , where 大きさ is "size" and 大きい is "big." So, 長い is "long" and 長さ is length .

meaningMnemonic: Life that comes out of the earth is made up of different kinds of material s. Sometimes it's cloth , sometimes it's dough , but everything has to be made out of something.

sentences.english: deal with a large number, to accumulate a lot of experience

meaningMnemonic: When you're the number one in a number in a series , you're number one ba-bay! readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 私にとって一番大切なのはお金です。

sentences.japanese: 今週のテストで一番高い点数をとりたいです。

sentences.japanese: これが、今全米で一番人気の曲ですよ。
sentences.english: This is the most popular song in all of America right now.

meaningMnemonic: When you're number two in a number in a series you're number two . Not quite as good as being 一番 , but take what you can get, you know? This word can refer to something ranked second in comparison to other things, or it can specifically refer to something marked with the number two, like an athlete with the number two on their jersey.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 私はエントリーナンバー二番です。

sentences.japanese: 高校のボートレースで二番になりました。
sentences.english: We won second place in the high school regatta.

meaningMnemonic: A number letter isn't a letter like the ones you're reading now, it's more like a numeral , like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 数字を入力するのが下手です。

sentences.japanese: アラビア数字の８の形が、一番すきです。
sentences.english: The shape of the Arabic numeral 8 is my favorite.

meaningMnemonic: The anti versus ... You'd think this would be a double negative, but it's like a lot of other words where you have two similar words combined... it just means the same thing as those two words. In this case, the anti-versus of something would be the opposite . 反対 refers to something that's opposite in direction, position, or nature. In some cases, it can also mean opposition because disagreeing or resisting to something means someone is taking the opposite side on a matter.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to look like the opposite, to have something look backwards
to become the other way around

sentences.japanese: その考えには反対です。
あの、そのサンダル、右と左が反対ですよ。
sentences.english: Um, your right and left sandals are on opposite feet.

sentences.japanese: 父は、私がウォルマートでプロポーズすることを反対した。
sentences.english: My father was opposed to me proposing in a Walmart.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 向 means yonder , and this is its noun version, meaning over there . 向こう is used when speaking generally about something distant from yourself, whether it's a place, as in 向こうの山 (the mountain over that way ), or a person, as in 向こうの人 (the person on the other side ). Sometimes, it can even be used for time, like 向こう一週間 (the next week ahead).
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that with 向く , but here's a mnemonic for you in case you forgot: Over there , a cow is saying moo ( む ). It's way over there, though, so you can't see or hear it. Kinda makes you wonder: if a cow moos way over there and no one's around to listen, did it really moo at all?

the other side of the ocean
the other side of the glass
to be on the other side
to be on the other side
to come from the other side
to be able to hear from over there

sentences.english: to come from the other side

sentences.english: What can you see on the other side of the mountains?

sentences.japanese: 道の向こうのベーカリーでパンを二斤買いましょう。
sentences.english: Let's buy two loaves of bread at the bakery on the other side of the road.

sentences.japanese: 海外に行くと、毎回向こうの文化にインスパイアされるんですよ。
sentences.english: When I go abroad, I'm inspired by the culture over there every time.

meaningMnemonic: I am talking about my self , my own body … In other words, this is about me personally or what I myself have done. 私自身 literally means "I myself," and it's used to emphasize your personal involvement in something. For example, you may say 私自身の考え to highlight that something is your own thought, or 私自身から言う , to really stress that you'll personally be the one to say something to someone, without going through any intermediaries.
readingMnemonic: The readings are a bit weird here. The 私 is わたし , but the 自 and 身 use the readings you learned with the kanji. Just imagine the 私 saying to the other two, "I myself will use my vocab reading, but you two should use your kanji readings — got it?"

sentences.japanese: 私自身びっくりしている
私自身はコーヒーもお茶も両方のみます。
sentences.english: Personally I drink both coffee and tea.

sentences.japanese: 私自身で魚を切ったことはありません。
sentences.english: I have never cut fish myself.

sentences.japanese: 私自身は考古学を学びたいという思いが強いですが、他の人にはあまり分かってもらえません。
sentences.english: I personally have a strong desire to learn archeology, but others don't understand me.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. 絵 refers to picture s, such as painting s, drawing s, or illustration s.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

sentences.japanese: これは有名なピカソの絵です。

sentences.japanese: 家に絵が一つもないなんて、あなたはシリアルキラーか何かですか？
sentences.english: To not have a single picture in your house, are you like a serial killer or something?

meaningMnemonic: You already know that 手 means "hand," but it can also mean "doer," as in someone who performs a particular action or task. Why? Because we use our hands to do things. And when it comes to throw ing, the doer is the pitcher !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 手 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: To be a good pitcher , all you have to do is put the ball into the chute ( しゅ ). Pitchers don't actually throw the ball. There is an invisible pitching chute right on the mound. You slide the ball into the chute and off it goes!

sentences.english: My father is a professional pitcher.

sentences.japanese: 大谷氏は投手の名人でありバッターの名人でもあります。

sentences.english: The pitcher on the Mexican team is very strong.

meaningMnemonic: A location place is either a place or a location , just like the kanji it's made from.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for the first kanji and the on'yomi reading for the second. You haven't learned this reading for 場 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: What is this place you're in? You look around and listen. You hear, " Baa ( ば ) baa baa!" You must be in a ba rn!

sentences.japanese: 土の中から死体が見えたのが、この場所です。
sentences.english: This is the spot where the corpse was visible from the soil.

sentences.japanese: ファーストキスの場所はどこですか？
sentences.english: Where was the location of your first kiss?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Wondering how 所 differs from 場所 ? While 場所 only refers to a physical location, 所 can be more abstract and refer to a place, a point in time, or a certain situation or condition. This is why 所 usually needs some extra context to clarify what kind of "place" you mean.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic: You find yourself in a strange place full of toe colo gne ( ところ ). Bottles and bottles of toe cologne. Cologne for your toes, or toe-scented cologne? Either way, imagine the pungent smell. You don't know why a place like this exists, and you want to get out ASAP. This toe cologne place really isn't your scene. Note: This can be shortened to とこ in casual speech, so don't be surprised if you see it in that form too.

sentences.japanese: 分からない所があれば、手を上げてください。
sentences.english: If there's a spot you don't understand, please raise your hand.

sentences.english: My friend came over just as my mother was doing squats.

meaningMnemonic: The number of point s is how many points there are (aka the score ).

sentences.english: My older sister suggested that I give my teacher some donuts to raise my math score.

meaningMnemonic: This word is a little tricky — at first, the combination of mix and number in a series doesn't seem to add up to police box , but there's a catch. This word is actually an abbreviated combo of two other words: The 交 comes from 交替 (in rotation) and the 番 comes from 立番 (standing watch). A police box is basically a tiny community police station staffed by one or two officers. It's something that is not common in many Western countries, but it is pretty much all over Japan.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: Grandma, who always loses her way home, is a heavy user of the police box.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

meaningMnemonic: Use a number in a series to group the things you watch and listen to. That makes them your program s. Your TV and radio programs, specifically. If you watch TV you'll hear it a lot!

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Don't confuse this with the word 〜道 , though. This one doesn't have a 〜 at the beginning, meaning it's not attached to other words. This word is just plain old road. It has its own meaning!
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You're walking down the road. On the road , you bump into your friend, Mitch ( みち ). sentences.english: Part-time workers at convenience stores play a more important role in Japanese society than you think.

meaningMnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji with hiragana attached to it. That hiragana ends with い which means it's an adjective. So, what's the adjective form of the kanji that's in this word? 円 means both "yen" and "round" but in this case we're looking at the round one (because something isn't going to be "yenny"). The adjective version of round is round or circular . Just like a yen coin, this "round" is a flat round. As in, if you draw a circle on a piece of paper, you could use this word. Same goes with yen, which is why "yen" and "round" both use the same kanji.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: The reading for the 円 portion of this word is the same as a kanji you learned on level 2: 丸 . That kanji means something really similar to this kanji. And guess what? They also share a reading. So, if you know that the reading of 丸 is まる then you'll also know that the reading for this word is まる !

meaningMnemonic: Someone who does study for a living. That is a scholar .

meaningMnemonic: When a number of year s have passed you say that several years have passed! You don't want to say how many years, so just say several years.

meaningMnemonic: The road you walk on is the sidewalk ... at least I hope that's where you walk.

meaningMnemonic: The もなく part is like saying "there isn't even." So, when "there isn't even an interval of time ," things will happen soon or before long . You'll probably hear this the most in train announcements letting you know your train will shortly be arriving in Tokyo or wherever.
