sentences.japanese: 間もなく朝ごはんが出来ますから、テーブルの上にスプーンとフォークを出して下さい。
sentences.english: Breakfast will be ready soon, so please put spoons and forks on the table.

meaningMnemonic: This combines south and アフリカ , the word for "Africa." Put them together to get South Africa . 南アフリカ will almost always mean the country of South Africa, but in some contexts it'll occasionally refer to the wider region of Southern Africa .
readingMnemonic: The reading uses the kun'yomi for 南 , which you've already learned. Yay for geography! Now which continent was South Africa on again…?

sentences.japanese: 南アフリカではラグビーがとても人気です。
sentences.english: Rugby is very popular in South Africa.

sentences.japanese: 南アフリカに行ったら、ライオンが見たいです。
sentences.english: If I go to South Africa, I want to see lions.

sentences.japanese: イーロン・マスクは南アフリカのプレトリアで生まれました。
sentences.english: Elon Musk was born in Pretoria, South Africa.

sentences.japanese: バックパッカーをしていた時、ヒッチハイクで南アフリカの国々をまわりました。
sentences.english: When I was backpacking, I traveled around the countries of Southern Africa by hitchhiking.

meaningMnemonic: The sky interval is an area of the sky. In places that are just empty sky, there is only space . Of course, not technically... there's something there, but back in the day when kanji was being made, nobody knew that. This word can mean both space in regards to outer space as well as the space around you in your room.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 自分の家は安心できる空間の一つです。
sentences.english: Your own house is a safe space where you can relax.

sentences.japanese: アレルギーなので犬と同じ空間にいることが出来ません。
sentences.english: I can't be in the same space as a dog because I'm allergic.

sentences.japanese: 大学では、空間デザインを学びました。
sentences.english: At university, I learned spatial design.

meaningMnemonic: You've been getting madder ( まだ ) and madder, and you’re still mad. You’re not yet as mad as you could be, though. You can use まだ to talk about a situation that started in the past and continues into the present. Wait! Where are you going? I'm still explaining this! I'm not done yet!

sentences.japanese: それはまだ分からないよ。
え、まだトイレにいるの？
sentences.english: What, are you still in the bathroom?

sentences.japanese: ケンなら、まだシャワーしてるよ。
sentences.english: If you're looking for Ken, he's still taking a shower.

meaningMnemonic: If you've got an eye on a certain course , it's a subject you really want to take. Maybe you're in school and that means you'll be taking a lot of course s. Maybe you're a teacher and you're planning out your curriculum . Either way, you have your eye on the course-prize.
readingMnemonic: The readings are the on'yomi readings, but you learned the kun'yomi reading for 目 before. So, you have to remember that this word uses もく instead of め . To do that, imagine seeing that the subjects you're allowed to take next term are different than everyone else's. The other kids notice, and start mock ing ( もく ) you for it. Think of what those subjects are and how you're being mocked for having to take them.

sentences.japanese: 中学では九科目学びます。
sentences.english: In junior high school, you will study nine subjects.

sentences.japanese: どの科目のテストも全て八十点でした。
sentences.english: I got an eighty on the tests for all subjects.

sentences.japanese: お母さんは科学や数学などの科目の先生です。
sentences.english: Mom is a teacher of subjects like science and mathematics.

meaningMnemonic: You've seen that 代わる means "to substitute for" or "to replace." This is the noun version of that (no う sound on the end). So, what is the noun version of those verb words? It would be substitute or replacement .
readingMnemonic: You should be able to figure out the reading from learning 代わる in the previous level.

sentences.english: substitute for notepaper, substitute for notes
to be able to have another helping of food
there is another helping of food
to have another helping of food

sentences.japanese: 田中先生はお休みなので、代わりの先生が来ます。
sentences.english: Mr. Tanaka is off, so a substitute teacher will come.

sentences.japanese: トマトをあげた代わりに玉ねぎをもらった。
sentences.english: I got onions in return for giving tomatoes.

sentences.japanese: 代わりの人は中々見つからなかった。
sentences.english: I had a hard time finding a substitute person.

meaningMnemonic: An electricity talk . What is this witchcraft? The only way to talk via electricity is with a telephone .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 山下先生から電話です。
sentences.english: It's a phone call from Yamashita-sensei.

sentences.japanese: 電話で「ありがとう」とお母さんに言いました。
sentences.english: I told my mother "thank you" on the phone.

sentences.japanese: それ、正しい電話番号ではないよ。
sentences.english: That's not the right phone number.

meaningMnemonic: The body of a body is… the body ! 身体 is more technical-sounding than 体 . You may encounter it in contexts related to physical examinations, for example, or in discussions about someone's physical ability in an athletic context.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. This word can also be read からだ , which is irregular but shouldn't be too hard to remember because it's the same as the reading you already learned for 体 ! You'd usually use this reading in casual contexts, and when the word is on its own, rather than in a compound word. In formal situations and compounds, you'd want to stick to the regular old on'yomi reading.

sentences.japanese: 身体は元気ですが、心はボロボロですよ。
sentences.english: My body is fine, but my heart is tattered.

sentences.japanese: 母は生まれた時から身体が弱いんです。
sentences.english: My mother has had a weak constitution since she was born.

sentences.japanese: スポーツも大切ですが、身体を休めることはそれ以上に大切です。
sentences.english: Doing sports is important, but resting your body is even more important.

meaningMnemonic: The person count is the number of people . Don't confuse this with the "population" or something like that, though. This is more like "how many people are at this event?" What's the 人数 , you know?
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Note that rendaku turns すう into ずう , and since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Do you know the number of people at Nin tendo ( にん )? It's a big mystery, which is why they hired you to count every single one of them. Good luck!

sentences.english: number of students in the class
enough for the number of people

sentences.japanese: この会社のスタッフの人数は二十人です。
sentences.english: The number of staff at this company is twenty people.

sentences.japanese: 今週の出社人数は少し下がった。
sentences.english: The number of people coming to work has dropped a little this week.

sentences.japanese: 去年のイベントではスタッフの人数が足りなかったのに、今年は多すぎるくらいです。
sentences.english: There weren't enough staff at last year's event, but this year there are too many.

meaningMnemonic: この means "this", and you know what the word 前 means (front/before). The combination of these words, "this before" if you will, can mean a few different things. If we're talking about when something happened, the "before" meaning kicks in, and it means the other day or recently . If we're talking about location, then the "front" meaning kicks in, and it means in front of this .
readingMnemonic: The reading for 前 is the kun'yomi, like the reading for the vocabulary word 前 . So long as you know that word, you'll be able to read this one too. The reason it's not on'yomi is because it's like two words put together. The word この and the word 前 .

sentences.japanese: この前、木の上に毛虫がいたんです。
sentences.english: The other day, there was a caterpillar on the tree.

sentences.japanese: この前までは、ここには花や草やシイタケが生えてたんです。
sentences.english: Until recently, there were flowers, plants, and shiitake mushrooms growing here.

sentences.japanese: この前のテレビ番組に、あの女の人が出てました。
sentences.english: That woman was on a TV show the other day.

meaningMnemonic: When you pull something and "separate" ( 分ける ) it, you are making everything even. In a game, this would be a tie or a draw .
readingMnemonic: See the hiragana stuck in there? That's hinting that these use the kun'yomi readings. You learned the kun'yomi readings of these two kanji separately in the previous level, so if you know those you should know this word's reading as well.

sentences.japanese: 今日のゲームは引き分けだった。
本当は引き分けでも、私の心の中では、あなたが日本一です。
sentences.english: Even when it actually was a draw, in my heart you're the best in Japan.

sentences.japanese: 引き分けとは、両方のチームが同じ点だったということです。
sentences.english: A draw means that both teams had the same score.

meaningMnemonic: The time interval of time is just the time . As is often the case, if two similar meaning kanji are combined into one word, they tend to produce a word with a similar meaning. Excuse me, friend, what's the 時間 ? Note that 時間 can also be used as a unit of time measurement to mean hour (s). In this case, it's always used as a suffix — usually following a number or the question word 何 ( なん ).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to use the time to do something

sentences.japanese: JLPTまで、あと一日。時間が足りません。
sentences.english: One more day until the JLPT. I don't have enough time.

sentences.japanese: 今回の休みは、ゲームをする時間がたくさんあります。
sentences.english: In this holiday, I have plenty of time to play games.

sentences.japanese: 平日は毎日仕事ですが、週末には友人と楽しい時間をすごします。
sentences.english: I work every day on weekdays, but I have a good time with my friends on weekends.

sentences.japanese: ディズニーランドまで、バスで３時間もかかった。
sentences.english: It took three whole hours by bus to get to Disneyland.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means answer so the verb version means to answer .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading as you'd expect with all the hiragana, but luckily that's the reading you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this.

sentences.japanese: インタビューに答える
「はい」と答えるのに少し時間がかかった。
sentences.english: It took a little time to answer "yes."

sentences.japanese: アンケートに答えた代わりに、アイスクリームをもらいました。
sentences.english: In return for answering the questionnaire, I got ice cream.

sentences.japanese: 私は電話に出る時、先ず「もしもし」と答えて、自分の名前を言います。
sentences.english: When I answer the phone, I first answer "hello" and say my name.

meaningMnemonic: You've seen the word 出来る (to be able to do), which is the first part. Then the second part, 上がる means "to rise." So, think about it this way: once you're able to do something, you rise because you're finished. That's why this verb means to be finished .
readingMnemonic: The reading is a combination of the readings from 出来る and 上がる . So long as you were paying attention in lessons past, you should be able to read this word as well just by combining those other words.

sentences.japanese: 工作が出来上がるのに、三日かかりました。
sentences.english: It took three days for the crafts to be completed.

sentences.japanese: お茶は大体五分で出来上がります。
sentences.english: Tea will be ready in about five minutes.

sentences.japanese: 家は月末に出来上がります。
sentences.english: The house will be completed at the end of the month.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 交ぜる means to mix and that the kanji means mix as well. So, this probably has something to do with mixing things. This word means to be mixed . This is when something is mixed but it's not mixed by you. It's just being mixed. Think of it this way - the じ in 交じる is Jesus, who just uses Jesus magic to mix something. So, you're not mixing it. It's just when something is to be mixed .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as with 交ぜる . So long as you know the ま portion of that word's reading, you'll be able to read this word as well.

sentences.english: to join a group of students
to join a group of adults

sentences.japanese: 白い毛の中に黒い毛が交じる。
sentences.english: Black hair is mixed in with the white hair.

sentences.japanese: コンビニで買ったサンドイッチに毛糸が交じっていた。
sentences.english: Some wool yarn was mixed in with the sandwich I bought at the convenience store.

sentences.japanese: たくさんの日本人の中に交じって今日も生きています。
sentences.english: Today I live among many Japanese people.

meaningMnemonic: This is a verb because it ends with an う sound. What does the kanji mean? It's music and bend . In the case of this word, we're going with the "bend" version. The verb of that is to bend . This is when you're doing the bending. You can remember this because げ kind of looks like the ge cko you're bending. That gecko looked good before you bent him in half.
readingMnemonic: How were you able to bend this gecko? Solo effort? No way! It actually took both you and your ma ma ( ま ) to make it happen! Just imagine you and your mighty mama, tag-teaming to bend a gecko in half!

sentences.japanese: 次は、足首を曲げるストレッチです。
sentences.english: Next is a stretch where you bend your ankles.

sentences.japanese: 父の大切な刀を曲げてしまった。
sentences.english: I accidentally bent my father's precious sword.

sentences.japanese: このYouTubeビデオでは、コウイチがスプーンを百本ひたすら曲げつづけます。
sentences.english: In this YouTube video, Koichi just keeps bending a hundred spoons.

meaningMnemonic: When duty ( 役 ) comes calling, those willing to stand ( 立つ ) and accept it are the ones who are going to be useful to society. Don't run from your duties — stand up, face them, and prove yourself a useful member of the human race!
readingMnemonic: The reading for 役 is the one you learned with the kanji. The 立つ reading is that of the 立つ vocabulary, which you should be familiar with by now.

sentences.english: to be of use to society
to be of use to people

sentences.japanese: マスキングテープは、色々なことの役に立つ。
sentences.english: Masking tape is useful for various things.

sentences.japanese: 山下先生の助言は、人生の役に立つ。
sentences.english: Yamashita-sensei's advice is helpful for life.

sentences.japanese: あまりお役に立てず、すみませんでした。
sentences.english: I'm sorry that I couldn't be much help.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means buy so the verb form is to buy .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. If you remember your kanji readings, you'll be just fine.

sentences.japanese: 今日も朝、コンビニでコーヒーを買う。
sentences.english: I'm buying coffee at the convenience store in the morning today as well.

sentences.japanese: トイレットペーパーは平日に切れないよう、いつも多めに買います。
sentences.english: I always buy extra toilet paper so that we don't run out on weekdays.

sentences.japanese: 車も家も中古で買いました。
sentences.english: I bought both my car and my house used.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means change so you'd think the verb version is "to change," but it's a bit more specific. This word means to change form or to transform . 化ける means to change into something else, usually in a surprising and magical way. It's often used in stories where animals or spirits take on human forms. It can also describe transformations in real life that are so dramatic they feel unreal.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You try to transform. You want to turn into something awesome, like a dinosaur, but then *poof* you turn into a sheep. " Ba aaa," you say. "Baaa."

sentences.english: to transform oneself into a human
to transform oneself into a woman

sentences.japanese: 女も男もメイクで化けることが出来る。
sentences.english: Both women and men can be transformed with makeup.

sentences.japanese: タヌキは人間に化けるのが上手です。
sentences.english: Raccoon dogs are good at transforming into human beings.

sentences.japanese: 中古のポルシェが三年後に一千万円に化けたって本当ですか？
sentences.english: Is it true that a used Porsche turned into ten million yen after three years?

sentences.japanese: 私の家は一年間のリノベーションで国宝レベルの家に化けた。
sentences.english: My house was transformed into a national treasure-level house with a year of renovation.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means count , so obviously the verb version is to count .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You begin to count vocabulary words. You're out of control and you can't stop. One after another. Scientists have to come in, but they can't figure out the cause ( かぞ ) of your counting. They drag you away to a padded cell where they keep testing you trying to figure out the cause of your craziness.

sentences.english: to count the number of people
to count the number of times

sentences.japanese: 父は毎日夜になるとベッドの中で羊を数える。
sentences.english: My father counts sheep in bed every night.

sentences.japanese: 前回のデートでは、二人で青空に見える風船を数えた。
sentences.english: On our last date, we counted the balloons we could see in the blue sky together.

sentences.japanese: 先生はその時教室にいた学生の数を数えました。
sentences.english: The teacher counted the number of students in the classroom at the time.

meaningMnemonic: You see something, then you "separate" ( 分ける ) it. This is the same thing as to distinguish , to tell apart , or to recognize . This verb is transitive, so you're doing the action to something. You're distinguishing between things or people.
readingMnemonic: You should know the reading of 見 already. The second part, 分ける is a word you should have learned in the previous level. Combine that knowledge together and you get the reading for this word.

sentences.english: the trick to telling something apart

sentences.japanese: 兄弟を目の色で見分ける。
sentences.english: I tell the brothers apart by their eye colors.

sentences.japanese: あの男が言ったことが本当かどうか見分けるなんてムリだよ。
sentences.english: It's impossible to tell whether what the man said is true.

sentences.japanese: ダイヤモンドと石ころを見分けることは出来ますか？
sentences.english: Are you able to distinguish between diamonds and stones?

meaningMnemonic: When you do ( する ) versus , you choose to face an opponent. It’s where your attention and efforts are going to be directed toward . Alternatively, you can use this word to contrast one thing with another. This word is used to help point out the relationship between two things in a sentence, where one thing is focusing on another thing. This is all a little vague and perhaps confusing, so check out the collocations and context sentences to get a better grasp of this word!
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, so you should be able to read this word no problem.

sentences.japanese: 自分に対するダメ出し
人に対するアドバイス
子どもに対してやさしい
ドルに対する円のレートは、今いくらですか？
sentences.english: How much is the rate of the yen compared to the dollar now?

sentences.japanese: 以上が、米国との外交に対する見方です。
sentences.english: Above is my perspective on diplomacy with the United States.

sentences.japanese: 先生のロボット工学に対する考えを教えて下さい。
sentences.english: Please tell me your thoughts on robot engineering.

sentences.japanese: あいつらの関係が修復不可能だってことは明らかだね。だって、スタートレックに対する意見が全く違っているんだから。
sentences.english: It’s clear now that their relationship will never work because their opinions on Star Trek are the complete opposite.

meaningMnemonic: Because this word ends with an う sound, you can tell it's probably a verb. The kanji portion means near . The verb version of that is to draw near , to get close or to approach . Essentially, the general idea is that you're getting closer to something. You're becoming more nearby. You're approaching.
readingMnemonic: There's hiragana attached to this kanji, which means it's probably the kun'yomi reading (and it is). You've seen the kun'yomi reading via the word 近い . So, as long as you know that word, you should be able to read this one as well.

sentences.english: to get close to the end

sentences.japanese: それ以上、川に近づくな！
sentences.english: Don't get any closer to the river!

sentences.japanese: この犬は、大人の男が近づくと、立ち上って「ワン！」と言います。
sentences.english: This dog gets up and says "woof!" if an adult man approaches him.

sentences.japanese: 来週、九州に台風が近づきます。
sentences.english: Next week, a typhoon will be approaching Kyushu.

meaningMnemonic: You know that the kanji 当 means right or success . So since this is a verb, you're doing right and success (which doesn't make much sense). Instead, you're guessing something and getting it right. So, this word means to guess something. Hopefully you don't have to guess too hard when it comes to the meaning of this word as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading can be remembered via the word 当たる which you learned a few levels ago. Use that knowledge to remember that this word is read as あてる . The important part is the あ .

sentences.english: to put one's hand on something
to put something against one's ear
to put something against one's mouth

sentences.japanese: 父は安いお茶と高いお茶を当てるのが上手です。
sentences.english: My father is good at guessing if tea is cheap or expensive.

sentences.japanese: 大谷氏は、バットにボールを当てる天才です。
sentences.english: Mr. Ohtani is a genius at hitting the ball with the bat.

sentences.japanese: 私には電話番号で、その人の未来のことを当てる力があります。
sentences.english: I have the power to guess a person's future by their phone number.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means help so the verb version is to help . Don't confuse this with 助かる which means "to be helped." You know that 助ける is "to help" because you're doing the helping. You know that you're doing the helping because you care ( ける ).
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You need to help someone. Someone is hanging off a cliff and out of reach. They ask you, the person standing above them, to toss ( たす ) them a rope, but you refuse. "TOSS IT!" they yell. "I WILL NOT TOSS IT," you respond. You're a jerk.

sentences.japanese: 私は、その馬を助けるために川に入りました。
sentences.english: I went into the river to help the horse.

sentences.japanese: お金が一円足りないんです。助けてもらえませんか？
sentences.english: I am one yen short. Can you help me?

sentences.japanese: あなたが、あの雨の日に助けてくれたおかげで、今の私がいます。
sentences.english: Thanks to you saving me on that rainy day, I am who I am today.

meaningMnemonic: The East capital in Japan is Tokyo . If you look on a map and compare it to Kyoto (the old capital), you'll see it lies to the east. That's why this is the east capital, Tokyo.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn the on'yomi for 東 ( とう ) with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help: How do you know you've made it to Tokyo ? The station platform signs will say 東京 — とう きょう — Tokyo. Just look for those とうきょう signs if you're headed for the east capital.

sentences.english: Tokyo is amusing, Tokyo is interesting

sentences.japanese: 私の会社から東京タワーは見えますよ。
sentences.english: You can see the Tokyo Tower from my office.

sentences.japanese: ハワイから東京に行きます。
sentences.english: I'm going from Hawaii to Tokyo.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means dwell , so the verb version means to live , to reside , or of course to dwell . Basically, someone is living somewhere. Where do you live?
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have a place to live... but not for long. You are being sue d ( す ) out of your house and home so you will have nowhere to dwell .

sentences.english: to live in an apartment building

sentences.japanese: 来年から、東京に住むつもりです。
sentences.english: I'm planning to live in Tokyo next year.

sentences.japanese: 海外に住んでいる人でも、日本のクレジットカードは作れますか？
sentences.english: Can people who live abroad make a Japanese credit card?

sentences.japanese: 中国に住んでいる時に、末の妹が生まれました。
sentences.english: When I was living in China, my youngest sister was born.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means pass through so the verb vocab version means things like to pass through , to pass by , and to travel along .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: As you try to pass through a narrow space, you stub your toe on something and scream " TOE! OH ( とお )!" In your haste to to pass by , you didn't properly check your surroundings, and you slammed your poor toe into something really hard. It hurts like heck, and you spend the rest of your day limping around, whimpering, "toe… oh…"

sentences.english: a car passes through, a car passes by
someone passes through, someone passes by

sentences.japanese: 竹の林を通って、会社に行きます。
sentences.english: I pass through a bamboo forest on my way to work.

sentences.japanese: 三丁目のコンビニの前は、毎日通りますよ。
sentences.english: I pass by the convenience store in 3-chome every day.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 思う means "to think" and 出す means "to take out." So this is what happens when your brain takes a moment to think and pulls a memory out of storage. It means to remember ! You can shout 思い出した！ when you recall your keys are in the fridge. (Again?!) You can also say 母を思い出します when something reminds you of your mom. In Japanese, you usually omit what reminded you of the memory because the important thing is the memory itself, filling your heart with touchy-feelies. Oh, mama!
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the kun'yomi readings. You should know the words 思う and 出す and their readings, so you should be able to read this word if you know those words.

sentences.english: to be reminded of one's father

sentences.japanese: たまにプロポーズされた日のことを思い出す。
sentences.english: I sometimes remember the day when I was proposed to.

sentences.japanese: やっと心理学の先生の名前を思い出した。
sentences.english: I finally remembered the name of the psychology teacher.

sentences.japanese: この辺りに来ると、小さかった時を思い出します。
sentences.english: Coming to this area reminds me of when I was small.

meaningMnemonic: You've seen the words 走る (to run) and 回る (to revolve). So, when you're running and revolving while you're doing it, you're running in circles. So, the verb form of that is to run around .
readingMnemonic: The readings are those like the words 走る and 回る . Make sure you know those words from before and apply that knowledge to read this word as well.

sentences.japanese: あちらこちらに走り回る
sentences.english: to run all over the place

sentences.japanese: グラウンドを走り回る
うちの犬は、雪を見ると走り回る。
sentences.english: My dog runs around when she sees the snow.

sentences.japanese: 夏休みは小さい子も大人も、ビーチで走り回る人が多いです。
sentences.english: During the summer vacation, there are many small children and adults running around on the beach.

sentences.japanese: 社長は今日も会社の中で走り回っています。
sentences.english: The president is running around in the company today as usual.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means talk so the verb version of this is to talk or to speak .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Whenever you begin to speak , 花 s ( はな ) flutter out of your mouth and fill the room. You're just such a good speaker, and you use such beautiful, flowery language that literal 花 s fly out of your mouth when you talk. Your breath must smell lovely.

sentences.english: What do you want to talk about?

sentences.japanese: 道で他人と話すことは、ほぼありません。
sentences.english: I rarely talk to others on the street.

sentences.japanese: 今回のミーティングでは、主に米国の牛肉のことを話しました。
sentences.english: At this meeting, we mainly talked about American beef.

sentences.japanese: 毎日、ディナーの後に電話で友人と話します。
sentences.english: Every day, I talk to a friend over the phone after dinner.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means support so the verb version is to support .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You need to support someone. In order to support them, you grab two saws. One saw and another saw. It's a saw saw ( ささ ) combination good enough to do all the supporting you need - and maybe cut some supports too.

sentences.japanese: スタッフは、これからも社長を支える考えだ。
sentences.english: The staff's thought is to continue supporting the president.

sentences.japanese: 父は母や私を支えるために毎日仕事へ行った。
sentences.english: My father went to work every day to support my mother and me.

sentences.japanese: この石に、これ以上大きな木を支える力はありません。
sentences.english: This rock does not have the power to support a tree any bigger than this.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means throw so the verb version means to throw .
readingMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached, so you can bet it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn this reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're at a baseball game watching people throw balls around. But you're hungry so you call for a snack from a vendor. You raise your hand and they throw some na chos ( な ) at you. Oh no! Oh ouch! The nachos are hot and they hit you in the face. The vendor just threw a bunch of hot, sauced nachos at you! WHY?!

sentences.english: to throw a spoon, to give up in despair

sentences.japanese: これは、ボールを投げるエクササイズです。
sentences.english: This is a ball throwing exercise.

sentences.japanese: フリスビーがどこまで行くかは、投げる人の力によります。
sentences.english: How far the Frisbee goes depends on the strength of the person who throws it.

sentences.japanese: 人に向かってお金を投げるのは失礼ですよ。
sentences.english: It's rude to throw money at people.

meaningMnemonic: You've already learned 回る , which means "to revolve" or "to rotate," and this is the transitive version of that. You're doing the turning/rotating action on something else, so this means to turn something , to rotate something , or to spin something . To remember the difference, just think about how you might get sue d ( す ) if you started aggressively spinning one of those playground spinners while someone else's kids were playing on it. Pretty shady behavior.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 回る ( まわ ). So long as you know that word, you'll be able to read this one as well. Use both of these words together to remember their readings.

sentences.japanese: ノックの音の後、ドアノブを回す音がした。
sentences.english: After the sound of the knock, there was a sound of the doorknob being turned.

sentences.japanese: ぼくの兄はピザの生地を回す天才です。
sentences.english: My brother is a genius at spinning pizza dough.

sentences.japanese: もっとサーモンのおすしを回して下さい。
sentences.english: Please pass around more salmon sushi.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means point so the verb version is something you need to point your finger to do. Picture pointing your finger and pushing a lightswitch to turn something on , in this case the light. You won't be able to switch something on if you can't point your finger.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You aren't able to turn the light on with just one finger though, you need to use two ( つ ). Either you have really weak fingers, or that's a really strong lightswitch. Either way, you need two fingers to switch on the light.

sentences.japanese: 夜は車のヘッドライトを点ける。
sentences.english: I put the car headlights on at night.

sentences.japanese: 今すぐテレビを点けてください。
sentences.english: Please turn on the TV immediately.

sentences.japanese: ニュースをチェックするために、ラジオを点けました。
sentences.english: I turned on the radio to check the news.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 向く means "to face" or "to turn towards", and this verb is related. This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. It's when someone turns or points something. That something doesn't just turn on its own. So this verb means to turn something towards or to point something at . In order to remember that this word means "to turn something towards," focus on the け . You have a bottle of ketchup in your hands and you're turning it toward your worst enemy to spray them. Picture yourself pointing the ketchup toward them.
readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is the same as 向く which you learned in a previous level. As long as you know that one you should be able to learn this one's reading as well.

sentences.english: to turn one's feet towards something
to turn one's eyes towards something
to point a camera at something

sentences.japanese: もう少し後ろに向けることは出来ますか？
sentences.english: Can you turn it towards the back a little more?

sentences.japanese: スマホじゃなくて子どもに、目を向けてあげて下さい。
sentences.english: Please look at your child, not your smartphone.

sentences.japanese: 来年の夏のJLPTに向けて活用形を学んでいます。
sentences.english: I am learning the conjugation forms for the JLPT next summer.

meaningMnemonic: You would think that an electricity car was an electric car, but this word actually refers to a different kind of vehicle that's often powered by electricity: a train . Literally, 電車 refers to an electric train rather than a diesel or steam locomotive. But in everyday Japanese, people often just use it as a general word for "train," since most modern trains in Japan run on electricity anyway.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: あの赤い電車は、東京まで行きますか？
sentences.english: Does that red train go to Tokyo?

sentences.japanese: 電車を写す用のカメラは、中々高いですよ。
sentences.english: Cameras for taking pictures of trains are quite expensive.

sentences.japanese: 朝の電車の時間のスケジュールは、この紙を見て下さい。
sentences.english: Please look at this paper for a schedule of morning train times.

meaningMnemonic: A water road carries your water supply . In the old days, these were called aqueduct s.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: to turn off the water supply

sentences.japanese: 一日も早く水道から水が出るようにしたいんです。
sentences.english: I want to get the water running as soon as possible.

sentences.japanese: この辺の水道の水は、人が口にして平気ですか？
sentences.english: Is it okay for people to drink the tap water in this area?

sentences.japanese: プールの中の水は、水道の水と雨水が大体半分半分です。
sentences.english: The water in the pool is about half tap water and half rainwater.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how words beginning with ど are often question words, and words ending in こ refer to places? This one's no exception, so どこ means where .
All of someone's body is their whole body or entire body .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to spread through the entire body
to grow on the entire body
to circulate around the entire body

sentences.japanese: 一日に一回、全身にスプレーして下さい。
sentences.english: Please spray over your whole body once a day.

sentences.japanese: 毎日、全身ビジネススーツで会社に行きます。
sentences.english: Every day, I go to work in a business suit from head to toe.

sentences.japanese: カニのアレルギーで全身にたくさんの赤い点が出てしまった。
sentences.english: I had a lot of red dots throughout my body due to a crab allergy.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading, but that's the reading you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this one too.

sentences.japanese: この森には大きい木がたくさん有ります。
sentences.english: There are many large trees in this forest.

sentences.japanese: 森の中を歩くのは、とても楽しいです。
sentences.english: Walking in the woods is very fun.

sentences.japanese: 森が見える場所に家を作りたいと思っています。
sentences.english: I want to build a house where you can see the forest.

meaningMnemonic: Okay, so the kanji itself means buddy and so does the word, but it also means you as well. This is one of the several ways to say "you" in Japanese, and this one is kind of an "affectionate" you. Maybe you'd say it with someone you're close to. Maybe you'd say it with a girlfriend or boyfriend. You wouldn't want to use it with your boss or teacher, though. Make sure to keep that in mind. It's kind of like saying "hey buddy" or "hey you," after all.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Who's your buddy ? It's Kimmy ( きみ )! If you know a Kimmy, imagine her. If you don't, find a famous Kimmy or make up a Kimmy to imagine. You ask... is it you?? Wait, you're my buddy?

sentences.japanese: 君、もしかしてコウイチの妹？
sentences.english: Are you perhaps Koichi's younger sister?

sentences.japanese: 君の作るカレーが日本一だよ。
sentences.english: The curry you make is the best in Japan.

sentences.japanese: 君は私に毎日シャワーをあびる大切さを教えてくれたじゃないか。
sentences.english: You taught me the importance of taking a shower every day, right?

meaningMnemonic: The お is added to elevate someone in front of you. What do you call someone in front of you? That's right, you . Over time, this word has lost its sense of politeness, and nowadays it sounds very rough and often rude. This "you" is a good way to show anger, and some people also use it in very casual situations to show affection.
readingMnemonic: The reading for 前 is the kun'yomi, like the reading for the vocabulary word 前 . So long as you know that word, you'll be able to read this one too.

sentences.japanese: お前は一体ここで何してるんだ？
sentences.english: What the hell are you doing here?

sentences.japanese: 他人のことを「お前」と言うのは失礼ですよ。
これからもずっとお前と生きていきたいんだよ！
sentences.english: I want to spend my life with you!
